corpus_definition: To keep something in its original state.

forms.definition: the act of keeping something safe and in good condition
forms.example: The preservation of old buildings in Bukhara is very important.

syn.note: Very close; protection is more general and is about keeping something safe from harm.
Almost the same, used a lot for nature, forests and animals.
Easy, general word: looking after something.

ant.note: Destroying something so that it is gone or badly damaged.

forms.definition: jam made from fruit boiled with sugar
forms.example: My grandmother makes apricot preserves every summer.
forms.note: Belongs to preserve = keep food from going bad, not keeping a forest safe. Usually plural: preserves.

forms.definition: to keep something safe and in its original condition
forms.example: We must preserve the forest for our children.

syn.note: Easy and very common; protect is about keeping something safe from harm.
Easy, general word; preserve means keeping it the same for a long time.
Very close, used a lot for nature and energy.
Easy word: save an old building, save a language.
Related: keep something in good condition by working on it.

ant.note: Damage something so badly that it is gone.
Harm something so it is not in good condition.

forms.definition: kept in good condition for a long time
forms.example: The old walls of Khiva are very well preserved.
forms.note: Often used as 'well preserved'.

syn.note: Related: kept safe from harm.
Not broken or damaged; a little formal.

ant.note: Harmed and not in good condition.
Badly damaged, often only parts are left.

forms.note: No common adverb exists for this family.

people.definition: a chemical added to food so it stays fresh longer
people.example: This bread has no preservatives in it.
people.note: Belongs to preserve = keep food from going bad, not keeping a forest or building safe.

context.text: Our town wants to preserve its old mosque. The preservation work will take two years, and the builders hope it will stay well preserved for another hundred years.

reviewer_note: Food sense (preserves = jam, preservative) kept as other_meaning; map is about keeping places and nature unchanged.

corpus_definition: The feeling of being worried and needing to do many things.

forms.definition: a worried feeling when you have too much to do or must succeed
forms.example: He feels a lot of work pressure.
forms.note: Also means the physical force of pushing (air pressure, blood pressure).

syn.note: Very close and very common: 'stress at work'.
Pressure that makes you tired or close to breaking.
A nervous feeling, often between people.
Easy word: the feeling of being afraid something bad may happen.

forms.definition: to try hard to make someone do something they do not want
forms.example: My parents never pressured me to study medicine.
forms.note: British English also uses 'pressurize' with the same meaning.

syn.note: Easy, a little informal: 'Don't push me to decide now.'
Stronger: the person has no choice.
Softer: you give good reasons, not pressure.

forms.definition: to push something firmly with your finger or hand
forms.example: Press the green button to start the machine.
forms.note: Belongs to the physical meaning of pushing; pressure was first made from press.

forms.definition: feeling that you must do something or do it quickly
forms.example: I always feel pressured before exams.

syn.note: Very common, more about the feeling of worry.
Related: not having enough time.

ant.note: Calm and not worried.

forms.definition: needing to be dealt with now; urgent
forms.example: Finding a job is my most pressing problem.
forms.note: Belongs to press = demand action now (urgent), not the feeling of stress.
No common adverb exists for this family.

context.text: Before the university exams, Dilnoza was under a lot of pressure. Her parents did not pressure her, but she still felt pressured by her friends' high scores.

reviewer_note: Kept the stress sense; physical pressure only in a note. press and pressing are other_meaning. No affix claimed (-ure is not in the table).

corpus_definition: To make sure that something does not happen.
usage_note: prevent + someone/something + from + -ing: 'The rain prevented us from playing.' The object usually comes between prevent and from. Without from: 'prevent an accident'.

relations.note: Easy and very common: 'stop someone from doing something'.
Same pattern, a little informal: 'keep the children from fighting'.
Related: put something in the way so it cannot happen.
Formal: make something slower or harder, not stop it completely.
Let someone do something: 'allow us to play'.
Make it possible for someone to do something; a little formal.

context.text: Heavy rain prevented us from playing football on Sunday. Next time, a roof over the pitch will prevent the game from stopping.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: example 'Rain may prevent from playing' is ungrammatical; should be 'prevent us from playing'. kind changed from phrasal to phrase: 'from' is a preposition with the object in between (prevent sb from -ing).

forms.note: No noun exists for this family.
No verb exists for this family. 'precede' has a different root.

forms.definition: happening or existing before the one you are talking about now
forms.example: I did not like his previous job.

syn.note: Easy and very close.
Easy: the one just before this one: 'my last job'.
Used for people and roles: 'her former husband'.
Same meaning but more formal.
Formal: the one that comes just before, often in texts.

ant.note: The one that comes after this one.
Coming just after: 'the following day'.
Formal: happening after something else.

forms.definition: at an earlier time; before now
forms.example: She previously worked as a nurse in Andijan.

syn.note: Easy; usually goes at the end: 'I have seen it before.'
Easy and very close.
Formal; used for a past job, name or role.
Before a particular event: 'Call me beforehand.'

ant.note: At a time after now or after something.
After something has happened.

context.text: My previous apartment was near the bazaar. I previously lived there with my brother, but now I live alone near the university.

reviewer_note: No -ous affix claimed: removing it leaves no real word. precede is not family.

corpus_definition: A basic ****** that guides your behavior or actions.

forms.definition: a basic belief about what is right that guides how you act
forms.example: Honesty is an important principle for many people.
forms.note: Don't confuse with principal (= main, or the head of a school); they sound the same.

syn.note: Easy word; a belief can be about anything, a principle guides how you act.
Usually plural: 'family values'.
Easy word; a rule can come from other people, a principle is your own.
A level of good behavior you expect: 'high moral standards'.
A belief about how things should be in a perfect world.

forms.note: No verb exists for this family.

forms.definition: having strong beliefs about what is right and acting on them
forms.example: She is a principled teacher who never takes gifts from parents.

syn.note: Easy word: telling the truth.
Knowing and doing what is right.
A little formal, often about work: 'an ethical company'.

ant.note: Not caring about what is right; formal.

forms.note: No adverb exists. 'principally' comes from principal (= mainly), a different word.

context.text: My grandfather has one simple principle: always keep your promises. He is a principled man, and people in our mahalla trust him.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: definition has a masked word (******, probably 'belief'); copied as given. principle vs principal homophone trap noted.

corpus_definition: Happening or existing before a specific time.

forms.definition: the most important thing that you must deal with first
forms.example: My family is my first priority.
forms.note: Belongs to prior = first, more important, not 'earlier in time'.

forms.definition: to decide what is most important and do it first
forms.example: You need to prioritize your homework this week.
forms.note: Belongs to prior = more important (from priority), not 'earlier in time'. British spelling: prioritise.

forms.definition: happening or existing before a certain time or event
forms.example: I have a prior appointment this afternoon.
forms.note: Formal. 'prior to' means 'before': prior to the meeting.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little less formal.
Easy, everyday word.
Formal: coming just before.
Used for past jobs and roles: 'a former teacher'.

ant.note: Happening after.
Formal: coming after something else.

forms.note: No adverb exists. Use the preposition 'prior to' (= before): 'prior to the exam'.

context.text: Sorry, I can't come to the meeting at three. I have a prior appointment with my doctor in Chilonzor.

reviewer_note: priority and prioritize kept as other_meaning (importance, not time). Only one existing form, so context uses one.

corpus_definition: the thing that is most important and must be dealt with first

forms.definition: the most important thing that you must deal with first
forms.example: Her top priority is finishing the report before Friday.

syn.note: The thing you think about and care about most.
The thing you give most attention to.
Easy word: something you want to achieve.
Formal: being more important, so it comes first.

forms.definition: to decide what is most important and do it first
forms.example: When you have a lot of work, prioritize the urgent tasks.
forms.note: British spelling: prioritise. Noun for the action: prioritization.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Give most of your attention to something.
Put things in order from most to least important.

ant.note: Not give enough attention to something important.

forms.definition: happening or existing before a certain time
forms.example: I have a prior appointment this afternoon.
forms.note: Belongs to prior = earlier in time. priority comes from the older idea of 'first, more important'.
No adverb exists for this family.

context.text: This month my priority is the IELTS exam. I prioritize reading and writing every morning, and I watch films only at the weekend.

reviewer_note: prior (time) kept as other_meaning. No -ize affix claimed because removing it leaves no word; -ity on prior is transparent.

corpus_definition: A type of job that requires special training or education.

forms.definition: a type of job that needs special training or education
forms.example: Medicine is a very difficult profession.

syn.note: Easy, general word for any work you are paid for.
Formal, used on forms; any kind of job.
The jobs you do over many years of your life.
A job that needs skill with your hands, like a plumber or builder.
A job you feel you were born to do, like nursing or teaching.

forms.definition: the high skill and good behavior expected from a trained worker
forms.example: The hotel staff showed great professionalism.

forms.definition: to say that something is true, often when it is not
forms.example: He professed to know nothing about the money.
forms.note: Belongs to profess = claim or openly say, an older formal meaning, not 'job'.

forms.definition: connected with a job that needs special training
forms.example: You should get professional advice before you buy a house.
forms.note: Also a noun: 'She is a real professional.'

syn.note: Having a lot of skill or knowledge.
Good at a job because of training.
Having the right diploma or training.

ant.note: Doing something for fun, not as a paid job.
Not behaving in the right way at work.

forms.definition: in a skilled way, or as your paid job
forms.example: She sings professionally at weddings in Tashkent.

syn.note: With a lot of skill.
With skill. British spelling: skilfully.

ant.note: In a way that is not right for work.

people.definition: a senior teacher at a university
people.example: Our professor gave us a lot of reading for next week.
people.note: Made from profess = openly teach or declare, not from the 'job' meaning of profession.

context.text: Teaching is a respected profession in Uzbekistan. My sister is a professional English teacher, and she plans her lessons very professionally.

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same meaning merged into one map. The person noun 'a professional' is not repeated in People because it is already shown as the adjective.

gate_overrides.reason: unprofessionally is a real adverb listed under unprofessional in the Oxford Learner's Dictionary; missing from the gate lexicon.

corpus_definition: To help something happen or become popular.

forms.definition: activities that help sell something or make it popular
forms.example: The shop is running a special promotion this week.
forms.note: Also means moving to a higher job: 'She got a promotion.'

syn.note: Telling people about a product to sell it.
Attention from newspapers, TV and the internet.
The whole work of selling a product, not only adverts.

forms.definition: to help something become popular or happen, for example by advertising
forms.example: The company hired a firm to promote their product.
forms.note: Also means moving someone to a higher job: 'He was promoted to manager.'

syn.note: Easy: tell people about a product so they buy it.
Help something to happen or grow: 'encourage healthy eating'.
Help an idea or plan succeed.
Informal: make something bigger or better.
Make many people know about something. British spelling: publicise.

ant.note: Try to stop something from happening.
Formal: make it harder for something to happen.

forms.definition: used to advertise a product or event
forms.example: They gave out promotional T-shirts at the concert.

syn.note: Related: connected with buying and selling.

forms.note: No common adverb exists for this family.

people.definition: a person or company that organizes and advertises concerts or sports events
people.example: The promoter sold all the tickets for the concert in two days.

context.text: A new cafe in Samarkand wants to promote its plov. For the promotion, they give free tea to every customer and hand out promotional cards in the street.

reviewer_note: Kept the 'make popular / advertise' sense; the job sense (get promoted) is only in notes because it has the same spellings.

corpus_definition: Doing something right away without waiting.

forms.definition: the quality of doing something quickly and without delay
forms.example: We thanked the plumber for his promptness.

syn.note: Easy word: how fast something happens.
Being on time, not late.

ant.note: When something happens later than it should.

forms.definition: a message on a computer screen that asks you to do something
forms.example: Type your password when you see the prompt.
forms.note: Belongs to prompt = remind or help someone to act, not 'quickly'.

forms.definition: to cause someone to do something or make something happen
forms.example: The cold weather prompted us to go home early.
forms.note: Belongs to prompt = cause or encourage an action, not 'quickly'.

forms.definition: done quickly and without delay
forms.example: Thank you for your prompt reply.
forms.note: promptly is made from this adjective.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
Happening at once, with no wait at all.
Easy word; prompt is more formal.
Arriving or happening at the right time, not late.

ant.note: Taking a long time.
After the expected time.

forms.definition: quickly and without waiting
forms.example: Please answer the email promptly.
forms.note: Also means 'exactly at that time': 'The class starts promptly at nine.'

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
At once, with no wait at all.
Easy and informal.
Easy phrase, a little old-fashioned.
Formal phrase, common in letters.

ant.note: Taking a long time.
After the expected time.

context.text: The bank sent a prompt answer to my question. When my card stopped working, they promptly gave me a new one, and I liked their promptness.

reviewer_note: Headword is the adverb, so prompt (adj) is the derivational root. prompt as verb/noun (cause, computer message) kept as other_meaning.
